items.ex: A sequel is the next part of a story, like a movie, book, or show that continues from the first one. The word comes from an old root meaning to follow, like in sequence. So a sequel follows the original. Americans say the sequel to a movie, or the sequel was better than the original. It's also used jokingly for real life: part two of a story. Don't confuse it with prequel, which tells what happened before. It's a neutral word. For IELTS, it's great when you talk about films and books.
exs: Her lash lift was so good, she came back for the sequel: a full set.
The sequel was even funnier than the first movie.
I usually prefer original films, because sequels often feel like they're just repeating the same idea.

items.ex: I guess is a soft way to say I think, especially when you're not a hundred percent sure. The core idea is you're making a small guess instead of a strong statement. Americans use it all the time in conversation: I guess so, I guess you're right, I guess I'll go. It can also sound a little unexcited, like okay, if I have to. It's casual. For IELTS speaking, it's a natural filler that buys you thinking time, but don't use it in every sentence, or you'll sound unsure.
exs: I guess I'll add a few more lashes on the outer corner.
Are you coming tonight? I guess so, if I finish work early.
I guess the main reason I enjoy cooking is that it helps me relax after work.

items.ex: A hit is something that is very popular and successful, like a hit song or a hit show. The image is a ball that hits the target. Americans say it was a big hit, a huge hit, or the party was a hit with the kids. The pattern a hit with someone means those people loved it. The opposite is a flop, something that failed. It's casual and very common. In IELTS, use it when you describe a popular product, film, song, or event.
exs: The new lash style was a huge hit with my younger clients.
Your cookies were a hit at the party.
That TV show was a massive hit in my country, so almost everyone I know has watched it.

items.ex: Go on a date means to go out with someone you're romantically interested in, maybe for dinner, coffee, or a movie. A date here isn't a day on the calendar. It's a planned romantic meeting. Common patterns are go on a date with someone, go on a first date, and a blind date, which is when you meet someone you've never seen before. Americans also say go out with someone. It's casual and common. For IELTS, it's useful if you're asked about relationships or free time.
exs: My client is going on a first date tonight, so she wanted her lashes extra pretty.
We went on a date to a small Italian restaurant.
In my culture, people usually go on several dates before they introduce someone to their parents.

items.zh: 松了一口气的；如释重负的
items.ex: Relieved describes the good, relaxed feeling you get when something bad didn't happen, or a worry is finally over. Picture a heavy bag being taken off your shoulders. Patterns: relieved to hear or relieved to know something, and relieved that plus a sentence. The noun is relief, as in what a relief! Don't confuse it with relaxed. Relaxed is calm in general. Relieved always comes after worry. It's neutral. For IELTS, it's a precise feeling word that sounds more advanced than happy.
exs: I was so relieved when the client said the lashes didn't irritate her eyes.
She was relieved to hear that her test results were normal.
I remember feeling really relieved when I finally passed my driving test on the second try.

items.ex: Feel awful about something means you feel very bad or very sorry about it, usually because you think it was your fault. Awful means very bad, much stronger than bad. Patterns: feel awful about something, or feel awful about doing something. You'll also hear I feel terrible about it, which means the same thing. Americans use it to apologize sincerely: I feel awful about what happened. It's casual but warm. For IELTS, it's good for stories where you made a mistake.
exs: I feel awful about running late for your appointment.
She felt awful about forgetting her friend's birthday.
I once broke my neighbor's window by accident, and I felt awful about it for days.

items.ex: Make it up to someone means you do something nice to balance a mistake or something hurtful you did. Picture a scale: your mistake is on one side, so you add something good on the other side to make it even. The pattern is make it up to plus a person: let me make it up to you, how can I make it up to you? Don't confuse it with make up, which can mean invent a story, or makeup on your face. It's casual and very common.
exs: Sorry I had to reschedule. Let me make it up to you with a free refill.
He forgot our anniversary, so he's making it up to me with dinner.
When I miss a friend's event, I usually try to make it up to them by planning something special.

items.ex: Take someone out means you invite someone to go somewhere with you, usually to a restaurant or event, and often you pay. The image is leading someone out of the house for something fun. Patterns: take someone out to dinner, take someone out for a drink, take someone out for their birthday. It's different from ask someone out, which is asking for a date. In movies, take someone out can also mean kill or defeat someone, so context matters. It's casual.
exs: I'm taking my assistant out to lunch to thank her for a busy week.
My dad took us out for ice cream after the game.
For special occasions, my family usually takes my grandparents out to a nice restaurant.

items.ex: My treat means I'll pay for this. A treat is something special and nice, so when you pay for someone, you're giving them a little gift. Americans say it's my treat, this one's my treat, or dinner's my treat. You can also say it's on me. When someone else pays, you can say thanks for treating me. The opposite situation is split the bill. It's friendly and casual. For IELTS, it's natural when you describe going out with friends or family.
exs: Coffee's my treat today. You've been such a loyal client.
Put your wallet away. It's my treat.
When I go out with my younger cousins, I usually say it's my treat, because they're still students.

items.ex: Pick someone up means you go to a place to get someone, usually by car, and take them somewhere. The image is lifting something and taking it with you. Patterns: pick someone up from the airport, pick someone up at eight, and pick up something, like pick up groceries. With a pronoun, it goes in the middle: pick me up, not pick up me. The opposite is drop someone off. It's casual and very common.
exs: Can you pick me up after my last client at six?
I need to pick up my kids from school.
My father used to pick me up from school every day, so we had a lot of time to chat in the car.

items.ex: Lovely means very nice, beautiful, or enjoyable. It's a warm and friendly word. Americans use it for things, people, and experiences: a lovely evening, a lovely person, that's lovely. It can sound a bit more polite or old-fashioned in American English than in British English, where it's very common. Americans more often say great or really nice in casual speech. Still, lovely is perfect for thank-you messages. For IELTS, it's a nice alternative to good or nice.
exs: Your skin looks lovely today.
Thank you for a lovely evening.
The small town where I grew up is lovely, especially in spring when the flowers are blooming.

items.ex: I had a great time means you really enjoyed an event or an experience. Time here means the experience. Americans say it at the end of a party, date, or trip: thanks, I had a great time. Other versions are I had a blast, which is more casual and excited, and I had fun. Notice we use had, not spent. Don't say I spent a great time. For IELTS, it's a natural way to finish a story about a holiday or event.
exs: Thanks for the birthday lunch. I had a great time.
We had a great time at the beach this weekend.
We had a great time on that trip, mainly because the local people were so friendly.

items.ex: I wish shows that you want something to be different from reality, or something that probably won't happen. The grammar is special: you use a past form to talk about now. For example, I wish I had more time means I don't have enough time. I wish it would stop raining means I want it to stop. Americans also use I wish I could, as a polite way to say no. Don't confuse it with I hope, which is for things that are possible. It's common in all styles.
exs: I wish I could fit you in today, but I'm fully booked.
I wish this weekend would never end.
I wish I had started learning English when I was a child, because it would be much easier now.

items.zh: 和平常的任何一天一样
items.ex: Just like any other day means a completely normal day, with nothing special. Americans often use it at the start of a story, right before something surprising happens: it started just like any other day, but then. It's a great storytelling chunk. You can change the noun: just like any other Monday, just like any other job. It's neutral. For IELTS Part 2, when you describe an event, this phrase is a perfect, natural way to begin.
exs: It started just like any other day, and then a celebrity walked into the salon.
Today felt just like any other Tuesday.
It was just like any other morning, until I got a phone call that changed my plans completely.

items.ex: Ordinary means normal, usual, nothing special. Think of it as the regular order of things. Common partners are an ordinary day, ordinary people, and ordinary life. The phrase out of the ordinary means unusual or special. Compare it with normal. Ordinary often sounds a bit plain or boring, while normal just means expected. Extraordinary is the opposite: amazing. It's neutral. For IELTS, ordinary and out of the ordinary help you describe events more precisely.
exs: Most of my clients are ordinary working moms who want to save time in the morning.
It was an ordinary Saturday, nothing special.
I don't think I'm extraordinary. I'm just an ordinary person who works hard.

items.ex: A twist of fate is an unexpected event that changes your life in a big way. Fate means the power that seems to control what happens to you. A twist is a sudden turn, like a turn in a road. So, the road of your life suddenly turns. It can be lucky or unlucky. Americans say by a twist of fate, or in a strange twist of fate. It sounds a little dramatic and storytelling-like. For IELTS Part 2 stories, it's a memorable, impressive phrase.
exs: By a twist of fate, my first client in the US became my business partner.
In a strange twist of fate, they ended up working at the same company.
By a twist of fate, I missed my train and met my best friend on the next one.

items.ex: Crash into means to hit something hard while moving, often with a loud noise. Picture a car hitting a wall. Patterns: crash into something, like crash into a tree, or a car crashed into a pole. As a noun, a crash is an accident, like a car crash. Americans also use it in a fun way: crash at my place, which means sleep at my place for a night. It's common and casual.
exs: A delivery guy almost crashed into my salon door with his bike.
He was looking at his phone and crashed into a tree.
Many accidents in big cities happen because drivers crash into each other at busy intersections.

items.zh: 这听起来可能很疯狂，但……
items.ex: This may sound crazy, but is a way to introduce an idea that you think might surprise people. It prepares the listener, so your idea feels softer. Americans also say I know this sounds weird, but, or this might sound strange, but. It's casual and friendly. For IELTS speaking, it's a great opener when you give an unusual opinion or answer. It shows natural fluency and makes your answer more interesting.
exs: This may sound crazy, but I actually enjoy fixing other artists' lash mistakes.
This may sound crazy, but I'm thinking of moving to Alaska.
This may sound crazy, but I think the best way to relax is to clean my whole apartment.

items.ex: Fall in love means to start loving someone romantically. The image is falling: it happens to you, and you can't fully control it. The pattern is fall in love with someone. Past tense: fell in love. Americans also use it for things and places: I fell in love with this city. Be in love describes the state. Fall in love describes the beginning. A lighter casual version is have a crush on someone. For IELTS, it's great for places, hobbies, and people.
exs: I fell in love with lash art the first time I tried it.
They fell in love during college.
I fell in love with photography when my uncle gave me an old camera.

items.ex: Layoffs are when a company tells many workers they no longer have jobs, usually because of money problems, not because the workers did something wrong. The verb is lay off: the company laid off fifty people. Compare it with fire, which usually means someone lost their job because of their own performance. Americans hear it a lot in the news: tech layoffs, or there were big layoffs. It's neutral to slightly formal. For IELTS, it's useful for work and economy topics.
exs: A lot of my new clients work in tech, and some are worried about layoffs.
After the layoffs, the office felt very quiet.
In my opinion, layoffs are one of the biggest sources of stress for young workers these days.

items.ex: Be supposed to means something is expected or planned, but often it didn't happen. It's about rules or expectations. Patterns: I'm supposed to be at work, you're not supposed to park here, it was supposed to rain today. In the past, was supposed to usually means it didn't happen. Americans pronounce it quickly, like supposta. Compare it with should, which is more about advice. It's casual and very common.
exs: You're not supposed to get your lashes wet for the first day.
He was supposed to call me last night, but he forgot.
I was supposed to study medicine, but I changed my mind and chose design.

items.ex: Destiny means the things that are going to happen to you in the future, as if they were already decided. Think of a destination, the end point of a journey: same root. Americans say it was destiny, it's my destiny, or they were destined to meet. Compare it with fate. They are similar, but fate often sounds a bit darker, while destiny can sound more hopeful. It's a slightly serious, romantic word. For IELTS, use it when you discuss luck and life choices.
exs: Some clients joke that finding my studio was destiny.
They believe it was destiny that they met.
I don't really believe in destiny. I think our choices shape our future more than luck.

items.zh: 说点开心的；换个轻松的话题
items.ex: On a happier note is a phrase you use to change the topic from something sad to something more positive. A note here is like a musical note, the tone of the conversation. So you're changing the tone. Americans also say on a lighter note, or on a positive note. It's very useful in conversations and presentations. For IELTS speaking, it's a smooth way to move from a negative point to a positive one, which sounds very fluent.
exs: It's been a slow month. On a happier note, I just got two new regular clients.
The weather was terrible. On a happier note, the food was amazing.
Pollution is a big problem in my city. On a happier note, more people are cycling now.

items.ex: Guess what is a fun way to start sharing surprising news. You're inviting the listener to guess, but you don't really want them to. You just want their attention. Americans say guess what, or guess what happened. The listener usually answers, what? It's casual and friendly, often used with friends and family. For IELTS, use it carefully, mostly when telling a story in Part 2, because it makes your story lively.
exs: Guess what? I'm fully booked for the next two weeks!
Guess what happened at work today?
So I entered the contest without expecting anything, and guess what? I won first place.

items.ex: Generous describes someone who is happy to give money, time, or help to others, more than expected. It can also describe things that are large, like a generous portion of food. Patterns: generous with something, as in generous with her time, and it's generous of you. The noun is generosity. The opposite is stingy, or cheap in casual American English. It's neutral and very positive. For IELTS, it's perfect when you describe a person you admire.
exs: My client left a really generous tip.
The restaurant gives generous portions.
The person I admire most is my grandmother, because she's incredibly generous with her time and love.

items.ex: Ask someone out means to invite someone on a date. The image is asking someone to come out with you, romantically. Patterns: ask someone out, ask someone out on a date, and he asked me out. Compare it with take someone out, which is the actual going out, and invite, which is more general. It's casual and common. For IELTS, it might come up when you talk about relationships or social life.
exs: My coworker finally asked her crush out.
He was too shy to ask her out.
In my country, it's becoming more common for women to ask men out, which I think is great.

items.ex: Turn down means to say no to an invitation, an offer, or a request. Picture turning a card face down. Patterns: turn down an offer, turn down a job, turn someone down, or turn it down. With a pronoun, it goes in the middle: turn it down. It also means make quieter, as in turn down the music. It's more casual than decline or reject. For IELTS, use it when you talk about choices.
exs: I had to turn down a bridal party booking because I was too busy.
She turned down the job offer because the pay was too low.
I once turned down a job in a big city, because I wanted to stay close to my family.

items.ex: Look forward to means you feel happy and excited about something in the future. The image is looking ahead at something good coming. The big grammar point: to is a preposition here, so it's followed by a noun or an -ing verb. So we say I'm looking forward to seeing you, not to see you. In emails, I look forward to hearing from you is a bit formal. It's common in all styles and very useful for IELTS.
exs: I'm looking forward to seeing you at your next fill.
I'm really looking forward to the weekend.
I'm looking forward to traveling more once I finish my studies.

items.ex: See someone, in a relationship context, means you're dating them, often in the early stages. Americans ask, are you seeing anyone? which means do you have a boyfriend or girlfriend? Be careful: see a doctor means visit a doctor, and see you later means goodbye. So context matters. The progressive form is common: I'm seeing someone. It's casual, softer and less serious than be in a relationship.
exs: My client is seeing someone new, so she's booking more appointments.
Are you seeing anyone right now?
I'm not seeing anyone at the moment, because I'm focusing on my career.

items.ex: Afford means you have enough money, time, or ability to do or buy something. The main patterns are can afford something, can't afford something, and afford to plus a verb: I can't afford to buy a car. Afford is almost always used with can, could, or be able to. The adjective affordable means not too expensive. It's neutral. For IELTS, it's very useful for topics like housing, travel, and shopping.
exs: Some clients can't afford a full set every two weeks, so I offer smaller fills.
We can't afford a bigger apartment right now.
Many young people in big cities can't afford to buy a home, so they rent for a long time.
